titre: The Point in the Oceans Farthest From Any Land
accroche: If you fell into the water at this exact spot in the South Pacific, the nearest land would be 2,688 kilometers away, in any direction.
contenu_vulgarise:
Point Nemo lies in the South Pacific, roughly halfway between New Zealand's Chatham Islands and southern Chile, at 48°52.6' south latitude and 123°23.6' west longitude. From this spot, the nearest land is 2,688 kilometers away, in any direction: Ducie, in the Pitcairn Islands, to the north; Motu Nui, near Easter Island, to the northeast; and Maher Island, off Antarctica, to the south. These three pieces of land are themselves uninhabited, which means that no human being lives in an area of more than 22 million square kilometers around this point, a surface larger than Russia.

## A Geometry Problem, Not an Expedition

This position was not found by a navigator at sea, but calculated in 1992 by Hrvoje Lukatela, a Croatian-Canadian survey engineer. He was seeking to demonstrate the capabilities of a geospatial search software he had helped develop, and relied on the world data of the Digital Chart of the World to solve a geometry problem across the whole globe: find the point that maximizes the distance to the nearest coast. The idea had come to him from a known hypothetical problem, that of the “longest swim,” which asks from what point a sailor fallen overboard would have to swim the longest before reaching land.

## The Emptiest Place, and Yet One of the Most Targeted

This absence of any witness has made it, since 1971, the favorite destination of space agencies for deorbiting their spacecraft at end of life. Nearly three hundred vehicles, including the Soviet station Mir in 2001, have since been deliberately steered there during their atmospheric reentry, far from shipping and air routes. NASA plans to send the International Space Station there by 2031. The paradox is complete when you consider that the humans closest to Point Nemo at any given moment are often the astronauts flying over it at an altitude of 415 kilometers, closer than any sailor or inhabitant of the surrounding lands.

The place nonetheless keeps a mystery all its own: in 1997, underwater hydrophones of the American agency NOAA picked up there a deep, powerful sound, nicknamed “the Bloop,” which no one could explain. It was not until 2005 that researchers at the same agency identified it: not an unknown creature, but the roar of an icequake in Antarctica.

repere.texte: 2,688 kilometers separate Point Nemo from the three nearest lands, all three uninhabited, leaving an area with no humans at all larger than Russia.

carte.punch: At this exact spot in the ocean, the nearest humans are sometimes in space.
carte.idee: Point Nemo, calculated in 1992, is the point in the oceans farthest from any land: 2,688 kilometers in every direction. So isolated that it serves as a graveyard for nearly 300 spacecraft deorbited since 1971, and soon for the International Space Station.

quiz.question: How was the exact position of Point Nemo, the most isolated place in the oceans, determined?
choix: By a boat expedition that measured the distance to the surrounding lands
By a geospatial computer calculation, from coastline data from around the world
By triangulation between three military navigation satellites
By a US Navy survey during nuclear tests in the Pacific
quiz.explication: In 1992, survey engineer Hrvoje Lukatela used spatial geometry software and the world data of the Digital Chart of the World to calculate, without going to sea, the point farthest from any coast: a purely geometric problem, not a discovery of exploration.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What are the three lands nearest to Point Nemo, and what do they have in common?
choix: Ducie, Motu Nui and Maher Island, all three uninhabited
Hawaii, Tahiti and Easter Island, all three densely populated
Ducie, Motu Nui and New Zealand, linked by a regular shipping line
Maher Island, Antarctica and Chile, all three covered in ice
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Ducie, in the Pitcairn Islands, Motu Nui, near Easter Island, and Maher Island, off Antarctica, are the three lands nearest to Point Nemo, at 2,688 km, and all three are uninhabited.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why has Point Nemo become, since 1971, the favorite destination of space agencies for deorbiting their spacecraft?
choix: Because its shallow ocean depth makes it easier to recover debris
Because no human being lives there across an area of more than 22 million km², far from shipping and air routes
Because the waters there are much warmer all year, which speeds up the decomposition of debris
Because an international treaty bans all fishing activity there
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The absence of any witness across an area of more than 22 million square kilometers, far from shipping and air routes, makes Point Nemo a safe place to deorbit spacecraft with no risk to anyone.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the Bloop really, the deep sound picked up in 1997 by underwater hydrophones near Point Nemo?
choix: The sonar of an unidentified military submarine
A signal emitted by an end-of-life satellite falling back into the area
The roar of an icequake in Antarctica, identified in 2005
The call of a whale species not yet recorded
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Long unexplained, the Bloop picked up in 1997 was identified in 2005 by NOAA researchers as the roar of an icequake in Antarctica, not an unknown creature.
